walkthroughs.body_html:
New & Emerging Technologies — a core area of GCSE Design Technology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

New & Emerging Technologies brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with New & Emerging Technologies.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which product is the best example of the Internet of Things?
options: A thermostat controlled from a phone over the internet
A battery-powered torch
A wooden chair
A hand-cranked whisk
Designing a product to have a deliberately limited useful life
Recycling a product at end of life
Testing a product until it breaks
Withdrawing a product for safety reasons

mcqs.q: Which is a key benefit of automation in manufacturing?
options: Consistent quality and continuous operation
It removes the need for product design
It guarantees products will sell
It makes raw materials free

mcqs.q: What is the aim of a circular economy?
options: Keeping materials in use through reuse, repair and recycling
Selling products in circular packaging
Manufacturing only round products
Increasing landfill capacity

mcqs.q: Does automation always destroy jobs overall?
options: Automation removes the need for any human workers in a factory.
Planned obsolescence is the recycling stage of a product's life cycle.
It displaces some manufacturing roles but also creates jobs in programming, maintenance, design and logistics; the overall effect varies by industry and over time.
Automation is banned in UK factories for safety reasons.

mcqs.q: What makes a product part of the Internet of Things?
options: IoT products must include a built-in television screen.
Any product containing electronics counts as the Internet of Things.
Embedded sensors and connectivity that let it send and receive data over the internet, like a thermostat you control remotely from a phone.
Planned obsolescence is the recycling stage of a product's life cycle.

mcqs.q: Is planned obsolescence the same as a product naturally wearing out?
options: No — planned obsolescence is a deliberate design decision to limit useful life so customers buy replacements; natural wear is unavoidable degradation over time.
Planned obsolescence just means products eventually wear out by accident.
Planned obsolescence is the recycling stage of a product's life cycle.
IoT products must include a built-in television screen.
